segments.translit: tam evārthaṃ śrīherukaca[8]ryyāvagamena guṇḍarīpādā anyeṣu niḥsvabhāvaṃ pratipādayanti—
segments.translation: Through understanding the [conduct]{carya} of the glorious [Heruka]{p-heruka}, [Guṇḍarīpāda]{p-gundari} teaches others that this same matter is [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song: through understanding the [conduct]{carya} of glorious [Heruka]{p-heruka}, [Guṇḍarīpāda]{p-gundari} teaches others that ‘this same matter’ is [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ‘the realization of glorious Heruka’, with no word for conduct, and has him make others realize the absence of intrinsic nature.

flags.note: tam evārthaṃ … niḥsvabhāvaṃ pratipādayanti: I take niḥsvabhāvaṃ as predicate (‘teaches others that this same matter is without intrinsic nature’). It could also stand in apposition (‘teaches others this same point, the absence of intrinsic nature’). ‘This same matter’ presumably looks back to the preceding song. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rang bzhin med pa rtogs par byed pa, ‘makes [others] realize the absence of intrinsic nature’.

For śrīherukacaryāvagamena, ‘through understanding the conduct of glorious Heruka’, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has dpal he ru ka'i rtogs pa, ‘the realization of glorious Heruka’, with no word for conduct (spyod pa). The folio number [8] falls inside the word caryā; it is not translated.

segments.translit: tiyaṛetyādi | lalanā-rasanā-avadhūtikā nāḍyaḥ trināḍyaṃ cāpayitvā nirābhāsīkṛtya saiva pariśuddhāvadhūtikā nirātmayoginī | aṅkavālīti | aṅkaṃ svacihnaṃ sādhakāya dadāti | taṃ pālayati ca | athavā vicitrādilakṣaṇayogenānandādikramaṃ dadāti | punaḥ saiva tāvakasyāviratābhiyogād āśvāsaṃ dadāti | kamalakuliśam iti | bho yogivara samyakkuliśājasaṃyogaghṛṣṭau ānandasandohatayā | vikālim iti kālarahitāṃ mahāmudrāṃ siddhiṃ sākṣāt kuru | ata eva mahāsukha(khaṃ)lampaṭo 'haṃ bhāvakaḥ ||
segments.translation: “[Tiaḍḍā]{tiadda}” (tiyaṛa) and so on. The [channels]{nadi} are [lalanā]{lalana}, [rasanā]{rasana} and [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}: pressing the three channels and making them free of [appearance]{abhasa}, she herself is the purified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, the [Nairātmā]{nairatma} [yoginī]{yogini}. “[Embrace]{ankapali}” (aṅkavālī): she gives the aṅka, her own [sign]{cihna}, to the practitioner, and she protects (pālayati) it. Or else: through union with the characteristics beginning with [vicitra]{vicitra}, she gives the sequence beginning with [joy]{ananda}. Again, she herself gives comfort to your devotee, because of his unceasing effort. “[Lotus]{lotus} and [vajra]{vajra}”: O best of [yogis]{yogi}, in the rubbing of vajra and lotus rightly joined, through the milking of [joy]{ananda}, “in the [evening]{vikala}” (vikāli): directly realize the [accomplishment]{siddhi} of [Mahāmudrā]{mahamudra}, which is free of time (kālarahita). For this very reason I, the meditator, am greedy for [great bliss]{mahasukha}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [tiaḍḍā]{tiadda} as the three channels, lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtī; the yoginī who presses them free of appearance (the Tibetan translation: ‘very luminous’) is the purified avadhūtī, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}. The [embrace]{ankapali} is her giving the practitioner her own sign (aṅka) and protecting it, or giving the sequence of joys. ‘Evening’ (vikāli) he takes as ‘free of time’: [Mahāmudrā]{mahamudra}.

equations.en: the three channels, lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtī, pressed and made free of appearance
the purified avadhūtī, the Nairātmā yoginī
her own sign (svacihna), which she gives to the practitioner and protects (pālayati)
the sequence of joys beginning with joy, given through union with the characteristics beginning with vicitra
free of time (kālarahita): the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, to be realized directly

flags.note: Munidatta cites the song's tiaḍḍā as tiyaṛa; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ka mgo in both song and comment. I give the draft's tiaḍḍā in the lemma with his spelling in parentheses.

Who is ‘she’ (sā eva)? I take the gerunds cāpayitvā and nirābhāsīkṛtya as the yoginī's acts, as in the song (‘pressing the tiaḍḍā, yoginī’): she who presses the three channels is the purified avadhūtī. Also possible: ‘the three channels, once pressed and made free of appearance, are the purified avadhūtī’. trināḍyaṃ is an odd form (perhaps for trināḍīṃ). The Tibetan (byas pa de nyid) is equally open.

For nirābhāsīkṛtya, ‘making free of appearance’, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has shin du gsal snang du byas pa, ‘made very clear, luminous’: the opposite sense, as if reading atyābhāsī- or similar. I follow the Sanskrit.

In the gloss on ‘embrace’ the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has the lemma yan lag 'khyud la zhen pa, ‘clinging to the embrace’, and de yang skyod par byed pa, ‘and makes it move’, where the Sanskrit has taṃ pālayati ca, ‘and protects it’: either a Tibetan slip (skyod for skyong, ‘protect’) or a reading cālayati. It also has rnal 'byor pas, ‘by the yogin’, for yogena, ‘through union’.

tāvakasya, ‘to your [devotee]’, sits awkwardly beside ‘she gives’. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sgom pa pos, ‘the meditator's’, i.e. bhāvakasya, and the segment ends with ahaṃ bhāvakaḥ, ‘I, the meditator’; ta and bha are easily confused. I translate the printed text, but bhāvakasya (‘to the meditator’) is likely.

The third sentence (punaḥ saiva … āśvāsaṃ dadāti, ‘she gives comfort’) may be a third explanation of ‘give an embrace’; I have not listed it as a gloss. āśvāsa can be ‘comfort, relief’ or ‘breath’; the Tibetan dbugs 'byin pa (‘give breath, console’) allows both.

kuliśājasaṃyoga: read kuliśābja-, ‘vajra and lotus’ (the Tibetan has rdo rje dang chu skyes). ānandasandohatayā: sandoha is ‘milking’ or ‘abundance’; the Tibetan dga' ba la yang dag par 'jo ba, ‘milking fully in joy’, supports milking, which I follow. Where the Sanskrit has ghṛṣṭau, ‘in the rubbing’, the Tibetan has chags pas, ‘through attachment’.
The sentence beginning ‘O best of yogis’ has no finite verb until kuru, ‘realize’, after the lemma vikāli; I read it as one sentence interrupted by the lemma.

Last sentence: for mahāsukha(khaṃ)lampaṭo 'haṃ bhāvakaḥ, ‘I, the meditator, am greedy for great bliss’, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de'i phyir bde ba chen po gsal bar grags pa'i bdag ni dgongs pa'o, roughly ‘therefore I, clearly renowned for great bliss, am the intention’, apparently reading something other than lampaṭa (prakaṭa?) and bhāvaka. Shastri's (khaṃ) offers mahāsukhaṃ; the sense is unchanged.

segments.translit:
evaṃ vadati |
bho nairātmayogini tvayā vinā kṣaṇaikaṃ durvvāravegacapalatvāt prāṇavātadhāraṇe na samartho 'haṃ |
tathā cā[ga]maḥ—
utpādasthitibhaṅgeṣu antarābhavasaṃsthitiḥ |
yāvatī kalpanā loke vāyuś cittavijṛmbhitaṃ ||
tava vaktraṃ sahajānandaṃ punaś cumbayitvā kamalarasam iti [8ka] uṣṇīṣakamalamadhumadanaṃ paramārthabodhicittaṃ gurusampradāyād viramānandakāliñjarasamaye karomi(mī) |
tathā ca śrīhevajre—
abhavyaṃ ḍiṇḍimaṃ proktaṃ bhavyaṃ kāliñjaram ma[hat] |
segments.translation:
He speaks thus: “O [Nairātmā]{nairatma} [yoginī]{yogini}, without you I cannot hold the vital [wind]{vayu} for a single moment, for it is restless, with a force hard to check.” So scripture says:
“In arising, abiding and ceasing lies the continuance of [intermediate existence]{antarabhava}; whatever conceptual thought there is in the world is wind, the unfolding of the [mind]{citta}.”
Having kissed again your mouth, which is [innate joy]{sahajananda}, I make “[lotus nectar]{kamala-rasa}”, the intoxicating honey of the [uṣṇīṣa]{usnisa} [lotus]{lotus}, [ultimate]{paramartha} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, through the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}, at the [kāliñjara]{kalinjara} time of the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}. So in the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}:
“The unfit is called [ḍiṇḍima]{dindima}, the fit the great [kāliñjara]{kalinjara}.”
segments.note: Munidatta has the poet tell [Nairātmā]{nairatma} that without her he cannot hold the vital wind a moment. Her mouth is [innate joy]{sahajananda}; the [lotus nectar]{kamala-rasa} is ultimate bodhicitta, the intoxicating honey of the uṣṇīṣa lotus, made through the guru's lineage at the [kāliñjara]{kalinjara} (‘fit’, per the Hevajra) time of the joy of cessation (Tibetan: ‘joy of variety’).

equations.en: ultimate bodhicitta, the intoxicating honey of the uṣṇīṣa lotus
the fit (bhavya), per the Hevajra verse he quotes
the unfit (abhavya), per the Hevajra verse he quotes

citations.quoted: In arising, abiding and ceasing lies the continuance of intermediate existence; whatever conceptual thought there is in the world is wind, the unfolding of the mind.
citations.work: unidentified; Munidatta cites it only as āgama, ‘scripture’

citations.quoted: The unfit is called ḍiṇḍima, the fit the great kāliñjara.
citations.work: Hevajra Tantra (named by Munidatta as Śrī Hevajra)

flags.note: The quoted verse's syntax is loose. I read line 1 as ‘in arising, abiding and ceasing lies the continuance of intermediate existence’, as the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) does (bar do'i srid pa gnas pa). In line 2 the printed vāyuś cittavijṛmbhitaṃ gives ‘is wind, the unfolding of the mind’; the Tibetan rlung dang sems kyis rnam par byas, ‘made by wind and mind’, reads a compound vāyucitta-.

karomi(mī), ‘I make’: the object seems to be the lotus nectar, ultimate bodhicitta; after the song's pībami one might expect ‘drink’. The Tibetan byed par 'gyur, ‘comes to be made’, has the same verb.

Where the Sanskrit has viramānanda, ‘joy of cessation’, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sna tshogs pa'i dga' ba, ‘joy of variety’ (so again in cp.04.m5). It renders kāliñjarasamaye by sense, skal ba dang ldan pa'i dus su, ‘at the fortunate time’, and uṣṇīṣakamalamadhumadanaṃ as gtsug tor gyi pad+ma'i chang, ‘the liquor of the uṣṇīṣa lotus’. It quotes the Hevajra half-verse without naming the work.
cā[ga]maḥ and ma[hat] are Shastri's restorations; (mī) in karomi(mī) is his note on the manuscript's form. The Hevajra quotation is a half-verse only.

segments.translit:
padāntareṇa yoginyānuśaṃsām āha (anusasamāha)—
khepetyādi | kṣepāt svasthānayogāt sā bodhicittarūpā nairātmayoginī vilakṣaṇaśodhitā'nandena maṇimūlena mohamalāvaliptā bhavatīti | punas tasmin krīḍārasam anubhūya maṇimūlād ūrddhaṃ gatvā gatvā mahāsukhacakre antarbhavatīti | ataḥ kṛṣṇācāryyapādair abhihitaṃ
ehu so girivara kahia mai ehu se mahāsuha ṭhāva |
ekku raaṇi mahu sahaja khaṇḍa labbhai mahāsuha jāva ||
segments.translation:
With the next [verse]{pada} he speaks in praise of the [yoginī]{yogini}. “[Throw]{ksepa}” and so on: from the throw (kṣepa), that is, from union in her [own place]{svasthana}, she, the [Nairātmā]{nairatma} yoginī in the form of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, purified by [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana}, becomes, through [joy]{ananda}, through the [root of the jewel]{manimula}, smeared with the stain of [delusion]{moha}. Then, having enjoyed there the taste of play, going up and up from the root of the jewel, she is absorbed into the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}. Hence the venerable [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} has said:
“This I have called the best of mountains; this is the place of [great bliss]{mahasukha}.
In a single night I gain the [innate]{sahaja} portion, as far as great bliss.”
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [throw]{ksepa} as union in her own place: the yoginī is [Nairātmā]{nairatma} in the form of bodhicitta, who enjoys play at the [root of the jewel]{manimula} and rises to be absorbed into the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}. As printed, he says she becomes smeared with delusion's stain; the Tibetan translation has ‘unstained’, as the song does.

equations.en: the Nairātmā yoginī in the form of bodhicitta

citations.quoted: This I have called the best of mountains; this is the place of great bliss. In a single night I gain the innate portion, as far as great bliss.
citations.work: a dohā of Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), named by Munidatta; the collection is not named

flags.note: mohamalāvaliptā bhavati, ‘becomes smeared with the stain of delusion’, contradicts the song (lepa na jāya, ‘no stain clings’). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rmongs pa'i dri mas ma gos par 'gyur, ‘becomes unstained by the stain of delusion’, which points to mohamalānavaliptā: a negative has probably dropped out. I translate the printed text.

vilakṣaṇaśodhitā'nandena maṇimūlena: I read vilakṣaṇaśodhitā as agreeing with ‘she’, and ānandena and maṇimūlena as two instrumentals (‘through joy, through the root of the jewel’). The Tibetan takes a compound, ‘through the joy purified by vilakṣaṇa’ (mtshan nyid dang bral bas sbyangs pa'i dga' bas), and ‘from the root of the jewel’ (nor bu'i rtsa ba nas).

In Kāṇha's dohā, raaṇi may be ‘night’ (rajanī) or ‘jewel’ (ratna); mahu ‘by me, my’ or ‘honey, liquor’ (madhu); khaṇḍa ‘portion’ or ‘sugar’. I translate ‘in a single night I gain the innate portion’. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ro gcig nyid gyur chang ni lhan cig skyes / ji srid bde ba chen po'i dum bu long, ‘having become one taste, the liquor is innate; as far as may be, obtain the piece of great bliss’.

The Tibetan has 'gro zhing 'ongs pas, ‘going and coming’, for gatvā gatvā, ‘going and going [up]’, and ‘goes as far as the wheel of great bliss’ (bar du 'gro) for antarbhavati, ‘is absorbed into’. For yoginyānuśaṃsām Shastri notes the manuscript's anusasamāha; the Tibetan rnal 'byor ma'i bsngags pa, ‘praise of the yoginī’, supports anuśaṃsā.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena pariśuddhim āha—
sāsu ityādi | prathamaṃ tāvat yogīndreṇa devatāyogapūrvvakaṃ kāyavajra[ṃ] dṛḍhīkṛtya vajrajāpopadeśena candrasūryyayoḥ pakṣagrahaṃ khaṇḍayitvā vāgvajraṃ sthirīkṛtya cittavajradṛḍhīkaraṇāya sā vira[9]mānandāvadhūtikā sahajānandaikalolībhāvaṃ na śvāsam āgāraṃ sumeruśikharaṃ nītvā | kuñciketi | tālasampuṭīkaraṇe maṇimūladvāranirodhaṃ karttavyam ātmānaṃ saṃbodhya svayam eva vadaty anupūrvvikāṃ |
tathā ca kṛṣṇācāryyapādāḥ—
jahi maṇa pavaṇa gaaṇa duāre diṭa tāla vidijjai
jai ta sughora andhām̐re maṇi diva ho kijjai |
jiṇa raaṇa uarem̐ jai ambaru chuppai
bhaṇai kahnu bhava bhuñjante nivvāṇa visissai ||
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as stages: deity yoga firms the vajra of body; vajra recitation breaks the moon's and sun's taking of sides, steadying speech; for mind, the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} is led to the ‘house of breath’ (śvāsa, perhaps echoing sāsu). [Key]{key} and [lock]{lock}: blocking the door of the [root of the jewel]{manimula}. The Tibetan has the poet claim perfect awakening.

equations.en: sealing the lock shut (tālasampuṭīkaraṇa): blocking the door of the root of the jewel
sealing the lock shut (tālasampuṭīkaraṇa): blocking the door of the root of the jewel

equations.src: pakhā (sides), of the braid of moon and sun (implicit)
equations.en: the taking of sides (pakṣagraha) by moon and sun, broken through the instruction in vajra recitation
the house of breath (śvāsa, āgāra), the summit of Sumeru

citations.quoted: At the door of the sky, where mind and wind are, a firm lock is set; if then, in the dreadful darkness, the jewel is made a lamp, if the sky touches upon the jewel of the Jina, Kāṇha says, while existence is enjoyed, nirvāṇa is accomplished.
citations.work: a verse of Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), named by Munidatta; the collection is not named

flags.note: sahajānandaikalolībhāvaṃ na śvāsam āgāraṃ: the na cannot be a negative here. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ro gcig pa'i ngo bos, an instrumental, pointing to -bhāvena; I translate so (‘merged into one with innate joy’). I read śvāsam āgāraṃ as ‘the house of breath’ with the Tibetan dbugs kyi khyim. The words seem to echo the song's sāsu gharem̐, ‘mother-in-law's house’, but Munidatta does not say so, so the equations for sāsu and pakhā are marked implicit.

The instrumental yogīndreṇa and the chain of gerunds depend on kartavyam, ‘is to be done’, which comes after the lemma kuñcikā; I have broken the chain into sentences. sā viramānandāvadhūtikā is nominative where nītvā wants an accusative. The Tibetan makes the avadhūtī the agent: ‘the avadhūtī … takes [it] to the house of breath, the summit of Sumeru’.

For ātmānaṃ saṃbodhya svayam eva vadaty anupūrvikāṃ, ‘addressing himself, he states the sequence himself’, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bdag nyid yang dag pa'i byang chub rang nyid kyis mngon sum du song ba smra bar byed do, ‘he declares that he himself has directly reached perfect awakening by himself’, taking saṃbodhya as saṃbodhi.

The Tibetan introduces the verse as the purification of the place (gnas yongs su dag pa); renders viramānanda as sna tshogs pa dga' ba, ‘joy of variety’; and in Kāṇha's verse has mi zad, ‘inexhaustible’, for sughora, ‘dreadful’, no ‘sky’ in the first line, and 'grub, ‘is accomplished’, for visissai.

In Kāṇha's verse, chuppai may be ‘touches’ or ‘is hidden’; uarem̐ ‘upon, above’ (upari) or ‘in the belly’ (udare); visissai ‘is accomplished’ (so the Tibetan 'grub) or ‘excels’ (viśiṣyate). The first line has no verb for mind and wind; the Tibetan supplies ‘enter’ ('jug pa).

segments.translit:
vajropamasamādhisākṣātkāraṇena siddhācāryyo hi guḍḍarī svayam eva anuśaṃsām āha—
bhaṇa ityādi | anyeṣāṃ sampradāyabahirmukhayoginīyogināṃ madhye kundureṇa | dvīndriyasamāpatti(ttiṃ)yogākṣarasukhena kleśārimarddanād vīro 'ham | punar api teṣāṃ madhye | cīram iti | yogīndracihnam aṣṭaguṇaiśvaryyādi mayoddhṛtam abhijñāsandarśanārthaṃ | 4 |
segments.translation: Because he has directly realized the [vajra-like samādhi]{vajropama-samadhi}, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Guṇḍarīpāda]{p-gundari} himself speaks his own praise. “Says” and so on: among others, [yoginīs]{yogini} and [yogis]{yogi} who have turned their faces away from the [lineage]{guru-sampradaya}, in [kundura]{kundura}, that is, through the [imperishable bliss]{aksara-sukha} of the yoga of union of the two organs, I am a [hero]{vira}, because I crush the enemy, the [afflictions]{klesa}. Again, among them: “[flag]{cira}”: the [sign]{cihna} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, the [eightfold mastery]{astagunaisvarya} and the rest, has been raised by me to display the [higher knowledges]{abhijna}.
segments.note: Munidatta has the poet, having realized the [vajra-like samādhi]{vajropama-samadhi}, praise himself: among yogis and yoginīs outside the lineage he is a hero in [kundura]{kundura}, the imperishable bliss of union of the two organs, crushing the enemy, the afflictions; his [flag]{cira} is the sign of the lord of yogis, the eightfold mastery and so on, raised to display the higher knowledges.

equations.en: the imperishable bliss of the yoga of union of the two organs (dvīndriyasamāpatti)
other yoginīs and yogis who have turned their faces away from the lineage
the sign of the lord of yogis (yogīndracihna), the eightfold mastery and the rest, raised to display the higher knowledges

flags.note: Munidatta writes the poet's name Guḍḍarī, without -pāda; I use the glossary's Guṇḍarīpāda.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) calls him slob dpon, ‘master’, without ‘siddha’; renders sampradāya by its parts, rab tu byin pa, ‘those fully given [the transmission]’; and spells kundura ku n+du ru (its quotation of the song has kun+Da re).

Last sentence: for mayoddhṛtam abhijñāsandarśanārthaṃ, ‘raised by me to display the higher knowledges’, the Tibetan has mngon du gyur pa mngon par shes pas mthong ba'i don, ‘made manifest, so as to be seen through the higher knowledges’, with no ‘by me’.

samāpatti(ttiṃ): Shastri gives samāpattiṃ as an alternative; the compound samāpattiyoga- makes better sense and matches the Tibetan (snyoms par 'jug pa'i sbyor ba). The closing numeral 4 marks the end of the comment on song 4 and is not translated.

proposals.definition: Throwing or casting (Sanskrit kṣepa; Old Bengali khem̐pa-, here an imperative). In song 4 the yoginī is told to throw; what she throws is not said. The Tibetan translation has 'phangs nas, ‘having thrown’, in the song and the comment. Munidatta takes the throw as union in her own place (svasthānayoga).

symbolicReadings.referent: union in her own place (svasthānayoga), from which she, the Nairātmā yoginī in the form of bodhicitta, enjoys play at the root of the jewel and rises to be absorbed into the wheel of great bliss

proposals.rationale: The draft's 3a has ‘Throw, yoginī’ without markup, but Munidatta gives the word an explicit reading (kṣepāt svasthānayogāt, cp.04.m4). An entry records the image, the Tibetan 'phangs, and his reading, and keeps the reading out of the line.

proposals.definition: ‘One's own place’ (svasthāna): a phrase in Munidatta's glosses for the proper seat of the yoginī or avadhūtī. He explains the yoginī's throw in song 4 as union in her own place (cp.04.m4); the Kāmaru entry records her own place in the wheel of great bliss (cp.02.m5).
proposals.rationale: Recurs in Munidatta's glosses (cp.02.m5, cp.04.m4) as a set phrase; an entry keeps its rendering consistent.

questions: cp.04.m4: Should the translation emend mohamalāvaliptā (‘smeared with the stain of delusion’) to mohamalānavaliptā (‘unstained’), with the Tibetan (ma gos par) and the song (lepa na jāya)? I kept the printed text, flagged it high, and say so in the note.

cp.04.m2: Emend tāvakasya (‘to your devotee’) to bhāvakasya (‘to the meditator’), with the Tibetan sgom pa pos? And is ‘she’ (sā eva) the yoginī who presses the channels (my reading), or the pressed channels themselves?

cp.04.m5: I read -bhāvaṃ na śvāsam āgāraṃ as -bhāvena, ‘merged into one with innate joy, to the house of breath’, following the Tibetan (ngo bos, dbugs kyi khyim). Is that acceptable, and should the sāsu/śvāsa echo stand in the note when Munidatta does not state it?

cihna: the approved rendering is ‘sign’, and I used it for svacihna (cp.04.m2) and yogīndracihna (cp.04.m6), but the ankapali, cira and abhijna entries say ‘mark’, which suits the aṅka wordplay better. Should cihna take ‘mark’ as a variant?
trivajra: I marked ‘vajra of body’, ‘vajra of speech’ and ‘vajra of mind’ with {trivajra}, whose English is ‘three vajras’. Add these as variants, or give each vajra its own entry?

The Tibetan renders viramānanda as sna tshogs pa'i dga' ba, ‘joy of variety’, in cp.04.m3 and m5, and the glossary already lists that as a viramananda form. Should the entry say this looks like a confusion with vicitra rather than a true equivalent?
Proposals: ksepa (‘throw’, the image of 3a, with Munidatta's reading) and svasthana (‘own place’). If ksepa is approved, the draft of 3a could carry [Throw]{ksepa}.
Names: I used the glossary forms Guṇḍarīpāda and Kāṇha where Munidatta writes Guḍḍarī and Kṛṣṇācāryapāda. Keep that, or let the commentary show his forms?
